candidates.quote: No book was so bad but some good might be got out of it.
candidates.author: Pliny the Younger
candidates.locator: Book III, letter 5, to Baebius Macer, where Pliny reports the maxim of his uncle Pliny the Elder; the capital N is the card’s, the clause standing inside quotation marks in the text
candidates.whyThisMonth: The gentlest possible instruction for a reader about to open something: no hour of reading is wasted, so begin.
candidates.translator: William Melmoth, revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet, 1909

candidates.quote: You must find your own quiet centre of life, and write from that to the world.
candidates.author: Sarah Orne Jewett
candidates.work: Letters of Sarah Orne Jewett, edited by Annie Fields
candidates.locator: to Willa Cather, 148 Charles Street, Boston, Sunday 13 December 1908, p. 249; the capital Y is the card’s and the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause
candidates.whyThisMonth: An older writer telling a younger one where the work has to come from, which is the exact shape of counsel: find the still place first, then speak from it.

candidates.quote: It is not enough to be industrious; so are the ants. What are you industrious about?
candidates.author: Henry David Thoreau
candidates.work: Familiar Letters of Henry David Thoreau, edited by F. B. Sanborn
candidates.whyThisMonth: Six in the morning is when a person is about to be busy, and this is the one question that decides whether the busyness will have been worth anything.

candidates.quote: In truth, whatever is worth doing at all, is worth doing well; and nothing can be done well without attention.
candidates.author: Lord Chesterfield
candidates.locator: letter of 9 October 1746, Old Style, from Bath
candidates.whyThisMonth: The proverb everyone half remembers, restored to the father who wrote it and to its second half, which is the part that actually tells you what to do.

candidates.quote: Let mystery have its place in you; do not be always turning up your whole soil with the plowshare of self-examination, but leave a little fallow corner in your heart ready for any seed the winds may bring.
candidates.author: Henri-Frédéric Amiel
candidates.work: Amiel’s Journal: The Journal Intime of Henri-Frédéric Amiel
candidates.locator: entry for 2 December 1851; the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause, the sentence running on in the text
candidates.whyThisMonth: Counsel against the morning habit of turning yourself over and over: leave one corner unexamined and see what grows there.

candidates.quote: Life is the art of drawing sufficient conclusions from insufficient premises.
candidates.author: Samuel Butler
candidates.work: The Note-Books of Samuel Butler, edited by Henry Festing Jones
candidates.locator: chapter I, Lord, What is Man?, the section Life, fragment ix
candidates.whyThisMonth: It forgives in advance every decision the day will demand on too little information, which is all of them.

candidates.quote: A maxim is the exact and noble expression of an important and unquestionable truth. Good maxims are the germs of all excellence. When firmly impressed on the memory they nourish the will.
candidates.author: Joseph Joubert
candidates.locator: no. 137, in the section Of Wisdom, Virtue, and Morality; the Pensées are extracts from Joubert’s private notebooks, published after his death
candidates.whyThisMonth: A maxim about maxims, for the month of them: it tells a reader why a single remembered sentence can carry a whole day.

candidates.quote: I am angry nearly every day of my life, Jo, but I have learned not to show it, and I still hope to learn not to feel it, though it may take me another forty years to do so.
candidates.author: Louisa May Alcott
candidates.whyThisMonth: A mother admitting the work is not finished after forty years, which is kinder counsel at six in the morning than any promise that it will be.
candidates.speaker: Marmee, to Jo March

candidates.quote: It’s been my experience that you can nearly always enjoy things if you make up your mind firmly that you will.
candidates.author: L. M. Montgomery
candidates.whyThisMonth: An eleven-year-old on her way to being sent back gives the plainest piece of advice in the book, and it is usable before breakfast.
candidates.speaker: Anne Shirley, to Marilla Cuthbert

candidates.quote: Two things everybody’s got tuh do fuh theyselves. They got tuh go tuh God, and they got tuh find out about livin’ fuh theyselves.
candidates.author: Zora Neale Hurston
candidates.whyThisMonth: The counsel a character gives on the way out of the door, said by a woman closing her own story: nobody can be told, they have to go there.
candidates.speaker: Janie Crawford, to Pheoby Watson

candidates.quote: The founding of libraries was like constructing more public granaries, amassing reserves against a spiritual winter.
candidates.author: Marguerite Yourcenar
candidates.locator: the section Tellus Stabilita; the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause, the sentence running on in the text
candidates.whyThisMonth: It makes reading a practical act rather than a refined one: you are laying up grain, and the winter is coming whether you do or not.
candidates.speaker: Hadrian
candidates.translator: Grace Frick, in collaboration with the author, 1954

candidates.quote: It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.
candidates.author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
candidates.whyThisMonth: This is the month’s theme in its purest form: the fox gives away his secret at the moment of parting, and the secret outlived him.
candidates.speaker: the fox, to the little prince

candidates.quote: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
candidates.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
candidates.whyThisMonth: The sentence the essay is known by, and the one a reader can act on immediately, before the day has offered a single opinion of its own.

candidates.quote: Read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; nor to find talk and discourse; but to weigh and consider.
candidates.author: Francis Bacon
candidates.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
candidates.whyThisMonth: From a book whose own title is Counsels: how to hold anything you read this morning, including this.

candidates.quote: Sweet words are like hony, a little may refresh, but too much gluts the stomach.
candidates.author: Anne Bradstreet
candidates.locator: no. IX, from the manuscript book headed For my deare Sonne Simon Bradstreet, dated 20 March 1664; the spelling hony is the edition’s own
candidates.whyThisMonth: A mother’s maxim written to be read after she was gone, which is the month’s subject exactly, and it warns against the flattery a day will offer.

candidates.quote: The most exhausting thing in life, I have discovered, is being insincere.
candidates.author: Anne Morrow Lindbergh
candidates.whyThisMonth: Practical counsel for the hours ahead, argued from fatigue rather than virtue, which is why it lands at six in the morning.
